items.prompt: Support insert(x) and remove_min() on a collection, both in O(log n), interleaved in any order.
items.why: Mixed inserts and min-extractions → priority queue. A sorted array with binary search finds the slot in O(log n) but shifting costs O(n); a stack only knows its most recent item.

items.prompt: For every index, return the next element to its right that is larger.
items.why: 'Next … to the right' is positional → monotonic stack, O(n). A heap gives the global min/max, not the next one.

items.prompt: Return the maximum of each window of size k as it slides across the array, in O(n).
items.why: Elements leave in window order → a monotonic deque gives O(1) per step. A heap needs lazy deletion and costs O(log n) per step, so it misses O(n).

items.prompt: Tasks have priorities and arrive over time. A single worker always takes the highest-priority waiting task. Output the processing order.
items.why: 'Always the most urgent of a changing set' → priority queue (max-heap via negation). A FIFO queue ignores priority.

items.prompt: Keep adding numbers from a stream; after each one, report the median of everything seen.
items.why: The median sits between two halves → a max-heap for the low half and a min-heap for the high half, kept balanced.

items.prompt: Combine n ropes into one. Each join costs the sum of the two lengths. Minimise the total cost.
items.why: Repeatedly take the two smallest of a set that keeps changing, and push the result back → min-heap. Sorting once isn't enough, because each joined rope has to go back into order.

items.prompt: Given an array whose values are between 0 and 100, return the values sorted.
items.why: A small known value range → count occurrences in an array of 101 buckets, O(n). A heap would add an unnecessary log factor.

items.prompt: Sort an array in which every element is at most k positions away from its sorted position, in O(n log k).
items.why: The next smallest element is always among the next k + 1 unplaced items → keep a min-heap of k + 1 items and pop/push as you go. A full sort costs O(n log n) and ignores the k bound.
